title: Strengthening University tech transfer capabilities to support circular economy value chains for plastics in Latin America – TechTraPlastiCE
text:
TipGoal of WP2



This WP will address the various types of responses to the needs of the industry and sectors for a circular economy by identifying University missions - research, innovation, lifelong learning, assistance, and services. Based on that, a collective portfolio for the plastics value-chain based on the university’s core competencies and knowledge will be created. This WP will also promote cross-peer collaboration and sharing of practices and knowledge among partners.




The objetive it to promote cross-peer collaboration and mentoring. You participation will be to encourage cross-peer collaboration and mentoring activities, allowing more experienced partners to transfer practices of delivering solutions and service on methodologies for portfolio implementation. This task will create matching possibilities among partners to help others advance according to their institutional needs and the opportunities they want to take advantage of.

title: Campo Limpio
text:
D1: Role in the Circular Economy
Where does this initiative fit in the plastics value chain?
How does this initiative contribute to keeping plastics in the loop?
Briefly describe its position in the value chain (e.g. post-consumer, industrial, production) and whether it combines with other circular strategies (recycling, eco-design, source reduction).
Campo Limpio operates at the post-consumer stage of the agricultural plastics value chain. Its main function is to ensure the recovery, traceability, conditioning and valorization of empty plant protection product containers once their primary useful life has ended. The initiative addresses a particularly sensitive plastic waste stream because the containers have held plant protection products and therefore require management that differs from that of other plastic waste.
Campo Limpio’s main contribution is to prevent containers from being abandoned, burned, buried or improperly reused by incorporating them into a formal reverse logistics system. Through the network of Temporary Storage Centers (CAT, Spanish acronym), containers are collected, sorted and sent to authorized operators for recycling or valorization. By May 2025, the system had recovered more than 18.5 million kilograms of empty containers, preventing this material from being dispersed into the environment.


D2: Regulatory Framework
What rules enabled, incentivized, or required this initiative?
What legislation, policies, or economic instruments (taxes, subsidies, EPR targets, voluntary agreements) enabled or drove this initiative? Was it voluntary or mandatory? Did it emerge before or after the regulatory framework?
Campo Limpio emerged as a direct response to National Law 27.279 on the Management of Empty Plant Protection Product Containers, enacted in 2016, and the only extended producer responsibility (EPR) law for packaging in Argentina.
The law establishes:

Extended Producer Responsibility.
Mandatory triple rinsing or pressure rinsing.
Mandatory return of containers.
Prohibition of abandonment, burning or burial.
Establishment of authorized management systems.
Restrictions on the end uses of recycled material.
Mandatory traceability.

Unlike many recycling initiatives that begin voluntarily and are subsequently regulated, Campo Limpio was created specifically to comply with this legislation. However, although the law establishes a hierarchy that prioritizes reuse over recycling, in practice the reuse of these containers is very limited due to health and environmental restrictions. Consequently, the main circular strategy implemented is the controlled recycling of recovered material.
It is also important to emphasize that the initiative is essentially mandatory. Companies that register plant protection products are legally required to finance and organize a management system for the empty containers placed on the market.

title: Benckmarking Study
text:
This WP will encourage multi-actor initiatives to enhance the reuse of plastic involving waste pickers’ organizations, companies, and the local public sectors, taking advantage of the University’s articulation capacities.


The present benchmark will address the involvement of key players in the circular economy challenge that overpasses the margins of industries’ actions: the waste pickers’ organizations and the local public sectors.
The university has a privileged neutrality position that facilitates the attraction, orchestration and articulation of diverse actors in a shared scenario to exchange possibilities and generate win-win situations.
This WP will sensitize on the critical aspects of the “reuse” issues, learning from developments in Europe and other parts of the world.
The identified problems involving multi-actors visions and roles are foreseen to be problems that are also faced in other countries and cities. The benchmarking will help to find inspiration in how similar multilevel problems have been approached to start identifying clues of actions. The benchmarking study will be structured as a public document available for all the partners.

title: Strengthening University tech transfer capabilities to support circular economy value chains for plastics in Latin America – TechTraPlastiCE
text:
This kick-off meeting marks the beginning of an exciting new project aimed at strengthening the role of universities in fostering green transitions within the plastic industry. By enhancing research and technological transfer capabilities, this initiative seeks to build sustainable collaborations between academia and socio-economic stakeholders in Colombia, Argentina, and Chile, promoting innovative circular economy practices and impactful recycling interventions. Through dynamic knowledge exchanges and progressive technology transfer, we aim to document valuable insights and develop interdisciplinary strategies that benefit both the global South and the European Union.

Date: March 25-28 / 2025
Time: 9:00 - 17:00
Location: Lorraine Fab Living Lab 49 Boulevard d’Austrasie, Nancy, France




The Lorraine Fab Living Lab® (LF2L®) is a platform for innovation acceptability and prospective usage evaluation supported by Engineering School ENSGSI and ERPI Laboratory of Université de Lorraine. It supports the creation and achievement of results through an established process based on the usage paradigm, bringing together advanced, complementary tools in a single space. More information
